facts: Brighton Palace Pier opened in 1899 and remains one of the most visited free attractions in England.
It replaced an earlier Victorian chain pier that had fallen into disrepair.
The pier features traditional funfair rides alongside arcade games.
The Royal Pavilion was built for the Prince Regent, later George IV, with a distinctive Indo-Saracenic exterior.
Its interiors combine Chinese-inspired and exotic decorative styles.
The building later served as a military hospital for Indian soldiers during the First World War.
Lewes Castle was one of the first castles built by the Normans after 1066, unusually with two mottes.
Lewes hosts one of the largest Bonfire Night celebrations in England, dating back centuries.
The town's steep High Street follows the original medieval street plan.
Smugglers Adventure is set within St Clement's Caves, a network of tunnels beneath Hastings' West Hill.
The caves have a genuine history linked to smuggling along the Sussex coast.
Hastings Old Town retains narrow medieval streets close to the seafront.
The dockyard is home to HMS Victory, Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar.
The Mary Rose, Henry VIII's warship, is displayed here after being raised from the Solent in 1982.
Portsmouth Harbour station sits right beside the dockyard and Isle of Wight ferry terminal.
Eastbourne Pier, opened in 1870, has survived several major fires including one in 2014.
The town developed as a genteel Victorian resort under the patronage of the Dukes of Devonshire.
Eastbourne's seafront is known for its well-preserved Victorian and Edwardian architecture.
Chichester Cathedral's spire is visible from far out at sea, historically used as a landmark by sailors.
It holds a rare modern tapestry by artist John Piper behind the high altar.
Chichester was originally a Roman town, Noviomagus Reginorum.
Bognor Regis gained its 'Regis' suffix after George V convalesced there in 1929.
The town hosts the International Birdman festival, where competitors attempt human-powered flight from the pier.
Bognor's beach has been a popular seaside destination since the 18th century.
Worthing Pier opened in 1862 and has been rebuilt several times after storm and fire damage.
The town developed as a fashionable resort after Princess Amelia, daughter of George III, visited in 1798.
Worthing sits on the West Sussex coast between Brighton and Chichester.
Shoreham Airport is the oldest purpose-built commercial airport still in operation in the UK.
Its striking Art Deco terminal building, from 1936, is a listed structure.
Shoreham-by-Sea sits at the mouth of the River Adur.
Box Hill hosted the cycling road race finish for the 2012 London Olympics.
The hill takes its name from the box trees that grow naturally on its chalk slopes.
It offers sweeping views across the Surrey Hills, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
Polesden Lacey was a favourite country retreat of society hostess Margaret Greville in the early 20th century.
The future King George VI and Queen Elizabeth spent part of their honeymoon there in 1923.
The house is now cared for by the National Trust.
Arundel Castle has been the seat of the Dukes of Norfolk for over 850 years.
It was significantly remodelled in the 19th century to its current dramatic Gothic appearance.
The castle overlooks the town and the River Arun.
Fishbourne Roman Palace is the largest Roman residence discovered north of the Alps.
It features some of the finest in-situ Roman mosaics in Britain.
The palace is thought to have been built for a local British client king soon after the Roman conquest.
Bosham is traditionally linked to the legend of King Canute commanding the tide to turn back.
The village's church appears in the Bayeux Tapestry, depicting Harold Godwinson's departure in 1064.
Bosham sits on a tidal creek off Chichester Harbour.
Goodwood hosts the Festival of Speed and the historic Goodwood Revival motorsport events.
The estate includes a racecourse, motor circuit and Goodwood House.
Chichester is the nearest railway station, with the estate reached by road.
The Spinnaker Tower, opened in 2005, stands 170 metres tall overlooking Portsmouth Harbour.
Its design was inspired by a sailing ship's spinnaker sail.
The tower includes a glass floor viewing platform.
Winchester's Great Hall holds a large medieval Round Table, long associated with the legend of King Arthur.
Winchester was the ancient capital of England under King Alfred the Great.
The city's cathedral has the longest nave of any Gothic cathedral in Europe.
Southampton retains one of the most complete sets of medieval town walls in England.
The Titanic departed from Southampton on her maiden voyage in 1912.
Southampton Central is the largest station on the South Coast line.
Herstmonceux Castle, built in the 1440s, is one of the earliest significant brick buildings in England.
It later housed the Royal Greenwich Observatory after it relocated from London.
Hampden Park is the nearest railway station, with the castle reached by road.
Bateman's was the home of author Rudyard Kipling from 1902 until his death in 1936.
Kipling wrote much of his later work, including Puck of Pook's Hill, at the house.
The house is now cared for by the National Trust.
Michelham Priory sits within the longest medieval moat in England.
It was founded as an Augustinian priory in 1229.
Berwick is the nearest railway station on the Sussex coast line.
Pevensey Castle sits within the walls of a former Roman fort, Anderitum.
William the Conqueror's forces landed near Pevensey in 1066 before the Battle of Hastings.
The castle was refortified as late as the Second World War against invasion fears.
The De La Warr Pavilion, completed in 1935, was one of the first welded steel-frame buildings in Britain.
It remains a leading example of International Style modernist architecture.
Bexhill hosted one of the first ever motor races held in Britain, in 1902.
The Bluebell Railway was the first standard-gauge steam railway in the world to be preserved as a heritage line, in 1960.
It runs through the Sussex Weald between East Grinstead and Sheffield Park.
East Grinstead sits at the southern edge of Ashdown Forest.
Ashdown Forest inspired the Hundred Acre Wood setting of A.A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh stories.
The Poohsticks Bridge, made famous in the books, is a genuine bridge within the forest.
Uckfield is the nearest railway station, with the forest reached by road.
Newhaven Fort was built in the 1860s to defend against a feared French invasion.
It remained in military use through both World Wars.
Newhaven's harbour connects to ferry services to Dieppe in France.
Gatwick is the second-busiest airport in the UK after Heathrow.
It was one of the first airports in the world to have a direct railway station built into the terminal, in 1958.
Gatwick sits on the Sussex-Surrey border.
Crawley was designated one of Britain's first post-war new towns in 1947.
The town was built to help house London's overspill population.
Crawley sits close to Gatwick Airport.
Horsham was once known for producing Horsham slabs, distinctive local stone roof tiles.
The town's Causeway is regarded as one of the finest historic streets in Sussex.
Horsham sits at the western edge of the Sussex Weald.
St Albans Cathedral has the longest nave of any cathedral in England.
It stands on the traditional site of Britain's first Christian martyr, St Alban.
St Albans was the Roman town of Verulamium, once the third-largest in Roman Britain.
John Bunyan wrote much of The Pilgrim's Progress while imprisoned in Bedford in the 1660s and 70s.
The Bunyan Meeting Free Church in the town is linked directly to his ministry.
Bedford is the northern terminus of the Thameslink core route.
Luton Hoo is a grand country estate, its house remodelled by Robert Adam in the 1760s.
The estate has hosted royal visits and film productions over the years.
Luton Airport Parkway serves both the estate area and London Luton Airport.
Elstree Studios has been used for major productions including several Star Wars and Indiana Jones films.
The studios have operated in the area since the 1910s, among the earliest in British film.
Elstree & Borehamwood sits on the Thameslink line north of London.
Olympia has hosted major exhibitions and events since 1886.
The venue's Grand Hall was one of the largest exhibition spaces in the world when built.
Kensington Olympia is served by an infrequent but useful rail link into west London.
Crystal Palace Park was built to house the relocated Great Exhibition building after 1854.
The park's Victorian dinosaur sculptures were among the first ever made.
The Crystal Palace itself was destroyed by fire in 1936.
The Derby, run at Epsom Downs since 1780, is one of the most prestigious horse races in the world.
The course gave its name to 'derby' as a general term for a major sporting fixture.
Epsom Downs station serves the racecourse directly, especially busy on race days.
Leatherhead sits on the River Mole in Surrey.
The town's museum occupies a 17th-century former courthouse.
Leatherhead is a key interchange for lines towards Guildford and Effingham Junction.
Redhill grew almost entirely because of its position as a key railway junction from the 1840s.
The town sits at the crossing point of routes towards Brighton, Reading and Tonbridge.
Redhill was historically part of the parish of Reigate before becoming its own town.
Reigate has a network of sandstone caves beneath the town, used historically for storage and shelter.
The town's castle mound survives, though little remains of the original castle.
Reigate sits at the foot of the North Downs.
Fairfield Halls has been a major concert and arts venue in south London since 1962.
Croydon is one of the largest commercial centres in Greater London outside the City and West End.
East Croydon is one of the busiest stations in the UK outside central London.
The Wimbledon Championships, held nearby, are the oldest tennis tournament in the world, first played in 1877.
Wimbledon Chase serves the residential area south of the main Wimbledon town centre.
The area is part of the London Borough of Merton.
Carshalton's ponds are fed by the River Wandle, one of London's few remaining chalk streams.
The village retains a number of historic watermills along the river.
Carshalton sits within the London Borough of Sutton.
Sutton developed rapidly as a London suburb following the railway's arrival in the 1840s.
The town is a major retail centre for southwest London.
Sutton sits on the edge of the North Downs.
Streatham once had one of the highest concentrations of cinemas of any London high street.
The area developed rapidly as a residential suburb in the Victorian era.
Streatham sits between Brixton and Croydon in south London.
Battersea Park was created on former marshland and opened to the public in 1858.
It includes a Peace Pagoda, built in 1985 as a monument to world peace.
The park overlooks the River Thames opposite Chelsea.
The RAF Museum at Hendon sits on the site of one of Britain's earliest airfields.
It holds one of the world's largest collections of historic military aircraft.
Hendon was a pioneering centre of British aviation from 1910 onward.
Lullingstone Roman Villa contains some of the best-preserved Roman mosaics in Britain.
Evidence suggests part of the villa was used as an early Christian chapel.
Farningham Road is the nearest railway station, with the villa reached by road.
Aldenham Country Park is built around a reservoir originally created to feed the Grand Union Canal.
The park includes a working farm and extensive woodland trails.
Radlett sits on the Thameslink line between St Albans and Elstree.
Tattenham Corner is the famous bend on Epsom racecourse where the Derby field turns for home.
The station was built specifically to serve racegoers on Derby Day.
Suffragette Emily Davison stepped in front of the King's horse near this corner in 1913.
